The dropped-factor hypothesis fails. Among time-rate failures, a missing factor appears in 6.5% of cases and an extra factor in the same 6.5%, so there's no asymmetry, and 82% fit neither pattern. This shows a mix of reasoning errors, not one dropped-quantity mechanism, so I'm closing that line.

The corrected constant analysis does leave one real descriptive result. Problems whose reference uses a number that's in neither the text nor earlier steps are 31% of DEV and score only 12.3% (-7.9 ± 1.6). The cleaner time-constant subset scores 8.8% (-10.6 ± 2.6), and answers include that constant only about half the time. But even answers containing it score only 15-19%, and this group is small (about 9% of problems). So the constant isn't the only limit, and the upside is small. I don't see a weight-level lever in it, and I'll record it as a difficulty finding.

Now back to L17 head 0, with a cheaper test before spending any pass. Sharpening can only help if the head already holds better information than the model uses. Pass 5 can answer that for free: at first-use number positions, I'll compare how often the head's attention-weighted digit vote names the correct digit with how often the model's top prediction does. If the head's vote beats the model's output, sharpening or re-weighting has room to help. If it's no better, the model already uses all the head knows, and I'll close the line without a pass. First I need to see how earlier blocks aligned these arrays, so I don't introduce an offset error.

I need the alignment convention from `block_21`, the analysis that produced the head statistics, before writing the digit vote. A shift of one position would make the comparison meaningless. So this step is only to read that code and the token layout, using a few decoded tokens as a sanity check, with no new statistic yet. Next I'll use the same convention to compare the head's vote with the model's top prediction.

`block_21` gives the convention. The query position is the token just before a number's first digit, and I can read the attention row at that position over the problem's digit spans. The output alignment still needs checking, so I'll measure directly whether `topk_ids[t]` predicts token `t` or `t+1`.

The test now covers every head at the four full-attention layers on the same events. For each one I'll compute the attention-weighted digit vote and compare it with three things: the model's own top prediction, chance (a uniform vote across the problem's numbers), and the key case of positions where the model is wrong. That last figure is the headroom: if a head's vote is correct well above chance when the model errs, it holds information that isn't reaching the output, and sharpening has a real rationale. If it sits near chance on those cases, the head knows nothing extra, and I'll close retrieval sharpening. I'll report the number of events too, since two texts give a modest sample.

The review refused that block, and it gives no reasons. My best reading is that the per-token vote was a way of predicting whether a planned sharpening edit would help, and the rules say to learn that from a forward pass instead. I won't retry it in another form, and I'm dropping that check.

The sharpening test itself remains valid, as a real pass built from weights alone. RMS normalisation cancels any uniform scaling of a query, so I need a different way to change one head's temperature. Some query dimensions have almost no gain in `(1+w_q)(1+w_k)`: they contribute little to the attention logits but still use up part of the RMS budget. Zeroing head 0's `q_proj` rows on those dimensions should free that budget for the rest. That would raise the head's logits nearly uniformly, and it's a head-level row edit, which the rules allow.

This step uses weights only. I'll look at the gain spectrum and each row's share of energy at L17, to see whether enough low-gain dimensions exist to give a useful temperature change. If low-gain rows hold, say, 30% or more of the energy at little logit cost, that's about a 1.2x sharpening or better, and worth a teacher-forced pass. If they hold almost nothing, this construction won't work and I'll close the line.
